The logic here is that markets at short horizons tend to exhibit some persistence, meaning yesterday's price is typically the best single predictor of today's price, while over longer horizons the estimate drifts toward a fundamental or trend-based anchor. Without a strong directional catalyst visible in the immediate data, I kept the drift conservative rather than projecting a sharp move in either direction.

The width of the confidence intervals expands systematically across horizons, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At 1 day, the 90% interval of roughly 108.8 to 114.2 captures normal intraday-to-overnight volatility and minor data surprises. By 1 week, the interval widens to 106.5–117.1, absorbing the possibility of scheduled macroeconomic releases, central bank commentary, or earnings events that could shift sentiment. At 1 month, the interval of 103–122 reflects a much broader range of plausible outcomes driven by cumulative news flow, changing rate expectations, and potential shifts in risk appetite. The interval widths are roughly consistent with an annualized volatility assumption in the moderate range, applied at each respective time horizon.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a worse-than-anticipated inflation print, a surprise recession signal, or a geopolitical shock — could drive prices well below the lower bound of the 1-month interval. A sudden liquidity event or credit stress episode could amplify moves sharply. On the upside, a dovish policy pivot from a major central bank, a stronger-than-expected growth surprise, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could push prices above the upper bound. Tail risks, by definition, are underweighted in any confidence interval, and black swan events — an unexpected financial institution failure, an escalation in a major conflict, or a pandemic-style shock — remain outside the modeled range but are non-negligible in real-world terms.
